results.title: Monte Carlo Confidence Interval Strategies
results.content: Monte Carlo methods use repeated random sampling to simulate and analyze complex systems and probability models. At its core, Monte Carlo simulation relies on generating a large number of random samples to approximate a desired statistical measure. The reliability of Monte Carlo confidence intervals heavily depends on the sampling strategy. A good Monte Carlo simulation starts with high-quality random number generation. Constructing confidence intervals using Monte Carlo simulations demands careful selection of the estimation technique. Modern statistical programming languages and platforms have built-in support for Monte Carlo simulations and confidence interval estimations. ### MATLAB Examples  MATLAB’s built-in functions offer another avenue for Monte Carlo simulation: - **randn and rand:** For generating random samples. --- ## Performance Analysis  Understanding the performance of Monte Carlo simulations is key to ensuring both the accuracy and efficiency of confidence interval estimation. Monte Carlo-based confidence interval estimation finds practical applications across various fields.

results.title: How Many Trades for a Backtest? Sample Size Calculator
results.content: The Statistical Sample Size Guide for Valid Trading Results. Most strategies need at least ~200 trades across ~7–10+ years covering multiple regimes to be confident you're not seeing a lucky sample. For meaningful strategy validation, you typically need many more trades as calculated by the sample size formula. Valid backtesting requires sufficient trades **AND** adequate time periods **AND** diverse market conditions. **BacktestBase helps you bridge this gap:** Upload your TradingView backtest, and we'll run 1,000+ Monte Carlo simulations to show you how your strategy performs across randomized trade sequences—giving you the statistical confidence you need before risking real capital. While 500 trades is statistically significant for win rate calculations, 2 years likely only covers one market regime. Options include: (1) Accept wider confidence intervals with 50-100 trades, (2) Test across multiple correlated instruments to increase sample size, (3) Use Monte Carlo stress testing to better understand possible variance, (4) Combine backtest results with strong theoretical justification for the edge.
